_meta.note: Cross-section spec for Article 3 Street/Road Type plates. Widths in feet (representative/typical, mid-range of each Type's design-standard ranges). Sprites are CC BY-SA 4.0 Streetmix assets vendored under sprites/ (see sprites/NOTICE.md). Surfaces: concrete=sidewalk, grass=planting/verge, asphalt=pavement, gravel=rural earth/sand blend, shoulder=asphalt-gray. 'raised':true lifts a segment one curb-height above the roadway. 'at' is the object's center as a fraction (0..1) across its segment. 'maindot':true replaces the ROW bracket with an illustrative-section note; pair with the plate's 'illustrative':true. 'standards' is the uniform 14-row design-standards set shown on each Type plate (these pages are the standards home; the comparison matrix has been retired). 'description' is the authoritative one-paragraph regulatory text for the Type; 'purpose' is the list of statement-of-purpose items shown under the page's PURPOSE heading (CZC 'To …' convention, mirroring the District pages); 'note' and 'footnote' carry Type-specific applicability statements shown together under the page's STANDARDS heading (note = cross-reference such as shopfront / state-aid; footnote = component/parking rule). The Type page layout mirrors the Article 2 District standards page: band, cross-section, two prose columns, and the full-width design-standards table at the bottom.

S1.footnote: A sidewalk is required both sides in D6 (§3.F.2).
S1.name: MAIN STREET
S1.context: D6 Town Center · designated D5 segments
S1.description: The most urban Street Type — the central organizing thoroughfare of the Town Center, with continuous building streetwalls, active ground-floor uses, wide sidewalks, on-street parking both sides, and the lowest design speed in the typology.
purpose: To establish the Town Center's principal civic and commercial thoroughfare, framed by continuous building streetwalls and active ground-floor uses.
To give pedestrians clear priority over vehicles, holding the lowest design speed in the typology (§1.a.4).
To complete the public realm with wide sidewalks, on-street parking both sides, and street trees, served from the rear by a Lane or Alley.
S1.note: Shopfront Required: a street classified S1 is a Shopfront Required street under Article 2 §4.C, subsuming the separate Shopfront Required overlay shown on the District Map. State route: like the R4 and R5 Types, S1 Main Street follows a State-owned named route (U.S. Route 1B); the Maine Department of Transportation holds jurisdiction over the traveled way within its right-of-way (see Section 12).
attributes: Buildings at the 0 ft setback line
On-street parking buffers the sidewalk from traffic
Planting strip and street trees both sides
Narrow travel lanes calm traffic
Rear-lot service via a Lane (S4) or Alley (S5)

S2.footnote: On-street parking is required where ground-floor retail is permitted (§3.F.3).
S2.name: VILLAGE STREET
S2.context: D5 Village Business · edges of D6 · SD-Historic core
S2.description: A village-center Street with mixed-use frontages, sidewalks both sides, and on-street parking on at least one side, at a design speed suited to pedestrian-prioritized village streets.
purpose: To support a compact, walkable village center by pairing mixed-use frontages with sidewalks and on-street parking along the travel way.
To resolve conflicts between vehicular and pedestrian movement in favor of the pedestrian, holding the design speed low (§1.a.4).
To frame the public realm with shallow setbacks, continuous street trees, and building entrances that meet the sidewalk.
S2.note: Shopfront by designation: an S2 segment may be designated Shopfront Required on the District Map and is then subject to the shopfront standards of Article 5 §12.
attributes: Detached and attached buildings at shallow setbacks
Primary entrances meet the sidewalk
On-street parking at least one side; may be both
Planting strips optional, either or both sides

S3.footnote: Street trees and on-street parking are provided by context under §3.F.
S3.name: NEIGHBORHOOD STREET
S3.context: D2 · D3 · D4 · SD-Historic outside center
S3.description: The most common village Street outside the Town Center, connecting residential and small-business neighborhoods with a sidewalk and planting strip on at least one side and a residential-scale design speed.
purpose: To connect Newcastle's residential and small-business neighborhoods at a comfortable, residential-scale design speed.
To provide for pedestrians with a sidewalk and planting strip on at least one side, scaled to the abutting District.
To accommodate on-street parking and street trees without widening the travel way beyond neighborhood scale.
attributes: Front setbacks consistent with the abutting District
Sidewalk required on at least one side
On-street parking permitted, one side
Street trees encouraged in the furnishing zone

S4.footnote: Street trees are provided where a planting strip is built (§3.F.4).
S4.name: LANE
S4.context: Internal blocks · D2 · D4 · D5 · D6 · SD-Historic · SD-Campus
S4.description: A narrow, low-speed Street internal to a block that provides building frontage and access on two yield-operated travel lanes, with a required sidewalk on one side; larger than an Alley (S5), on which buildings do not front.
purpose: To open block interiors to building frontage and access on a narrow, low-speed shared surface.
To provide pedestrian access with a required sidewalk on one side while holding vehicles to a yield operation.
To support compact, walkable block structure where a full Street is neither needed nor desired.
applies_in: D5 Village Business; D6 Town Center
attributes: Buildings front the Lane at shallow setbacks
Single shared surface; opposing vehicles yield
Optional parking one side; rolled or absent curbs
May “punch in” to open block interiors to frontage

S5.footnote: An Alley carries no required pedestrian components; the widths shown are minimums.
S5.name: ALLEY
S5.context: Internal service · D3–D6 · SD-Historic · SD-Fabrication · SD-Civic
S5.description: A narrow service street internal to a block, providing side- and rear-lot access for parking, loading, accessory buildings, and utilities; buildings do not front on an Alley.
purpose: To provide side- and rear-lot access for parking, loading, service, and utilities away from the primary Street frontage.
To keep service traffic, curb cuts, and utilities off the pedestrian-priority Streets — the only Street Type allowed for rear-lot access in D6.
To size the paved width and curb returns for delivery and emergency vehicles without inviting through-travel.
applies_in: Only rear-access type permitted in D6
attributes: No sidewalk and no on-street parking
Narrow paved width; functionally low speed
Tight curb returns sized for delivery & emergency vehicles
Only Street Type allowed for rear-lot access in D6

R1.footnote: A Road-family Type: the sidewalk and planting requirements of §3.F apply only where the segment abuts D5 or D6 frontage (§3.F.7).
R1.name: CONNECTOR ROAD
R1.context: D1–D2 transition · SD-Rural Highway secondary routes
R1.description: The most Street-like of the Road family, carrying through-travel in the rural-to-urban transition zone with shoulders rather than curbs, no continuous sidewalk, and a design speed higher than any Street Type.
purpose: To carry through-travel between villages and rural areas across the rural-to-urban transition zone.
To favor the vehicle while still accommodating occasional pedestrians and cyclists on shoulders rather than sidewalks (§1.a.4).
To manage drainage and roadside development at a rural scale, with ditches, culverts, and larger setbacks than on Streets.
attributes: Through-travel between villages and rural areas
Shoulders accommodate occasional pedestrians & cyclists
Drainage by ditches and culverts, not curb-and-gutter
Larger building setbacks than on Streets

R2.footnote: A rural Road-family Type: no pedestrian components are required (§3.F.7); the widths shown are minimums.
R2.name: RURAL ROAD
R2.description: The standard rural Road, providing access to working landscapes — farmland, forest, and conservation lands — with the narrowest standard pavement, no curbs, and drainage by open ditches.
purpose: To provide reliable vehicular access to working rural landscapes — farm, forest, and conservation lands — with the least practical land alteration.
To keep the rural Road narrow and unembellished, favoring the vehicle and rural character over urban streetscape elements (§1.a.4).
To limit impervious surface and preserve the open, ditch-drained character of Newcastle's rural Districts.
attributes: Paved or gravel, by segment and abutting use
Roadside vegetation generally preserved
Driveway entrances widely spaced (large D1 frontages)
Rural Lane (R3) is the lower-volume variant

R3.footnote: A rural Road-family Type: no pedestrian components are required (§3.F.7); passing pull-outs apply where ≤ 15 ft wide (§3.C.5).
R3.name: RURAL LANE
R3.context: D1 Rural · SD-Conservation · low-volume rural ways
R3.description: A low-volume rural yield roadway — the rural counterpart to the Lane (S4) — carrying the fewest vehicles in the Road family (generally under 400 per day) on a single shared surface or two very narrow lanes; the conforming designation for narrow historic two-rod (33 ft) ways.
purpose: To serve the lowest-volume rural ways on a single shared or very narrow surface, with the least practical land alteration.
To preserve roadside vegetation and the character of narrow two-rod ways, providing passing pull-outs in lieu of widening.
To bring existing narrow rural roads into conformance with this Code without urbanizing them.
applies_in: Low-volume rural ways & historic two-rod (33 ft) ROWs
attributes: Gravel or paved; drainage by open ditches, no curb
Roadside vegetation generally preserved
Passing pull-outs at ≤ 300 ft where ≤ 15 ft wide
Conforms existing narrow rural ways to the Code

R4.footnote: Cartway per MaineDOT (§12); the Town governs frontage, sidewalks, and access management, and §3.F applies where the segment abuts D5 or D6 frontage.
R4.name: HIGHWAY COMMERCIAL
R4.description: An auto-oriented commercial corridor where the cartway is designed and maintained by MaineDOT while the Town governs the frontage zone, setbacks, sidewalks (where feasible), and access management.
purpose: To accommodate auto-oriented commercial development along the Route 1 corridor where MaineDOT designs and maintains the cartway.
To secure pedestrian access and a coherent frontage where feasible, through Town control of setbacks, sidewalks, and access management (Article 2).
To manage curb cuts and entrances in coordination with MaineDOT (§12) so corridor safety and capacity are preserved.
R4.note: Most R4 segments are state-aid roads; the cartway follows MaineDOT geometry. See Section 12 for the MaineDOT coordination protocol.
attributes: Large commercial buildings at deep front setbacks
Sidewalks provided where feasible
Managed curb cuts; MaineDOT §704 entrance permits
Town governs frontage, setbacks & access (Art. 2)

R5.footnote: Cartway per MaineDOT (§12); rural character is preserved through vegetative screening and deep setbacks.
R5.name: RURAL HIGHWAY
R5.description: A high-speed regional corridor through rural and conservation contexts, where MaineDOT controls the cartway and the Town preserves rural character through vegetative screening, deep front setbacks, and tightly managed curb cuts.
purpose: To carry high-speed regional through-travel along the Route 1 corridor on a MaineDOT-controlled cartway.
To preserve rural and conservation character through vegetative screening, deep front setbacks, and tightly managed curb cuts.
To coordinate all cartway geometry and entrances with MaineDOT (§12) while the Town governs the frontage and screening.
R5.note: All R5 segments are state-aid roads; the cartway follows MaineDOT geometry. See Section 12 for the MaineDOT coordination protocol.
applies_in: US Route 1 rural corridor (all segments state-aid)
attributes: Vegetative screen required between cartway and development
Deep front setbacks measured from the centerline
Tightly managed curb-cut spacing
MaineDOT-controlled cartway geometry (§12)
